topicTitle: The Event Loop In-Depth: Microtasks vs Macrotasks

lessons.title: Call Stack & Event Loop Coordination
lessons.description: The event loop coordinates between the call stack and task queues — understanding this explains async execution order.

sections.heading: How the event loop works
paragraphs: The event loop is a continuously running process that checks if the call stack is empty, then processes tasks from the microtask queue, then the macrotask queue.
list: The call stack runs synchronous code one at a time
When the stack is empty, the event loop checks the microtask queue
Microtasks run to completion before any macrotask
Then one macrotask runs, and the cycle repeats

codeExamples.heading: Execution order demonstration
explanation: Macrotasks run after all microtasks are cleared.
This order is guaranteed by the event loop specification.

practice.task: Predict the exact output order of a code snippet with sync, microtask, and macrotask operations. Then run it to verify.
hints: Microtasks always clear before the next macrotask.

keyTakeaways: The event loop coordinates between the call stack and task queues.
Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) always run before macrotasks.
All microtasks clear before the next macrotask runs.
This explains the guaranteed execution order of async JavaScript.
lessons.challenge: Write code with 5 different async operations and predict their exact execution order.

lessons.title: Microtask Queue Execution (Promises, queueMicrotask)
lessons.description: Microtasks run after the current task and before any macrotask — they have the highest priority.

sections.heading: Microtask priority
list: All microtasks run to completion before the next macrotask
Microtasks can add more microtasks — they all run first

codeExamples.heading: Microtask chaining
explanation: All microtasks (micro 1, micro 3, micro 2) run before the macrotask.
queueMicrotask adds to the same microtask queue as Promises.
Microtasks are processed in FIFO order until the queue is empty.
Only then does the event loop pick up the next macrotask.
codeExamples.output: start, end, micro 1, micro 3, micro 2, macrotask

practice.task: Write code that creates a chain of 3 microtasks using queueMicrotask. Verify they all run before any setTimeout callback.
hints: Add a setTimeout to show when the macrotask runs.
All microtasks should appear before the macrotask.

keyTakeaways: Microtasks include Promise callbacks and queueMicrotask() calls.
All microtasks run to completion before the next macrotask.
Microtasks can enqueue more microtasks — they all run first.
This is why Promise.then chains run before setTimeout.
lessons.challenge: Explain why queueMicrotask is preferred over Promise.resolve().then() for simple microtask scheduling.

lessons.title: Macrotask Queue Execution (Timers, I/O Events)
lessons.description: Macrotasks include setTimeout, setInterval, I/O callbacks and UI rendering events.

sections.heading: What are macrotasks?
list: One macrotask runs per event loop iteration

codeExamples.heading: Macrotask scheduling
explanation: All three timers are macrotasks queued in order.
The microtask runs first because microtasks have higher priority.
Macrotasks run one at a time, with microtask checks between each.
Each timer callback is a separate macrotask.

practice.task: Create 3 setTimeouts with 0ms delay and 1 Promise. Predict and verify the execution order.
hints: Promise.then is a microtask — runs before all setTimeouts.
setTimeouts are macrotasks — run in FIFO order after microtasks.

keyTakeaways: Macrotasks include setTimeout, setInterval, I/O and UI events.
One macrotask runs per event loop iteration.
Microtasks always clear before the next macrotask.
This is why setTimeout(fn, 0) doesn't run immediately.
lessons.challenge: Build a task scheduler that prioritizes microtasks over macrotasks for critical updates.

lessons.title: Frame Rendering Synchronization & Task Starvation
lessons.description: Understand how the event loop coordinates with frame rendering and what happens when tasks block the loop.

sections.heading: Frame rendering and task starvation
list: Browsers target 60fps — each frame has a 16.6ms budget
The event loop must process tasks AND render within each frame
Long-running tasks starve rendering — causing jank
requestIdleCallback runs tasks during idle time between frames

codeExamples.heading: Task starvation example
explanation: A 100ms busy loop blocks rendering — the page becomes unresponsive.
Chunked work processes items in batches, yielding between chunks.
requestAnimationFrame ensures each chunk runs before the next paint.
This keeps the page responsive during heavy computation.

practice.task: Create a function that processes 10000 items without blocking the UI. Use chunking with requestAnimationFrame.
hints: Each chunk takes less than 16ms — the page stays responsive.

keyTakeaways: Each frame has a 16.6ms budget at 60fps.
Long tasks block rendering — causing jank and unresponsiveness.
Chunk heavy work with requestAnimationFrame to stay within frame budgets.
requestIdleCallback runs tasks during idle time between frames.
lessons.challenge: Profile a page with heavy computation and use chunking to eliminate frame drops.
